look_here_first: LITTLE BARLEY (Hordeum pusillum): short COOL-SEASON ANNUAL tuft and a tight, usually UPRIGHT barley SPIKE (~2–9 cm) with short mostly erect bristles. Follow ONE node on the central rachis: three ONE-FLOWERED spikelets sit together (fertile CENTRAL plus smaller mostly sterile lateral pair). The narrow outer GLUMES (~8–17 mm) stay comparatively straight/upright. FOXTAIL BARLEY also has three spikelets per node but is normally PERENNIAL with a broader nodding, huge long-outward-splayed featherlike head; ELymus wildryes have multiple florets within each spikelet.

best_field_traits: 1 — WHERE: look for a small short-lived native, winter/spring green annual emerging in small disturbed-ground tufts; measure the actual rooted basal plant, not one flowering culm.
2 — SILHOUETTE: terminal unbranched SPIKE, typically short 2–9 cm (FNA) and ~3–7 mm wide BEFORE bristles; usually erect and relatively tight/green-straw.
3 — TRIAD: inspect ONE rachis node with 10–20× lens. Hordeum groups THREE spikelets: the central one usually fertile and more complete, both smaller lateral spikelets mostly sterile.

4 — GLUMES: little-barley glumes usually straight/ascending and ~8–17 mm long including their awnlike length (FNA), with basal flattening on lateral glumes; unlike foxtail's 15–85 mm long, strongly splayed, bent glumes.
5 — AWNS: the FERTILE CENTRAL lemma has relatively short awn (~3.5–9.5 mm FNA; ranges vary), not the enormous silky radiating foxtail-barley glumes.

6 — NO AURICLES: leaf blade/sheath junction normally lacks little clasping ears in H. pusillum; inspect the short membranous ligule and hairy blade surfaces. Erect spike + leaf character alone does not prove species.
7 — FOXTAIL: Hordeum jubatum has usually PERENNIAL basal crown and a broad, sometimes purple-tinted, fluffy frequently nodding mature spike, with LONG outward-bent glumes.
8 — WILDRYE: Elymus canadensis/virginicus commonly have 2 or more MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets per rachis node; one-flowered central + sterile laterals is the Hordeum key.
9 — Avoid mixing terms: long showy bristles around a foxtail head can be GLUME awns, not just lemma awns; record their attachment under magnification.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: One spike rachis node showing 3 spikelets
Awn and glumes plus true ligule macro
crew_field_check: Secale cereale generally has one large two-flowered spikelet at each alternate node, not a barley triad. Introduced wall barley Hordeum murinum makes broader fan-like spikelet groups. Use floret and glume closeup.
morphology_keys.habit: Cool-season annual grass, loosely tufted and usually 10–60 cm tall. Native in Texas at state/ecoregion level; do not presume any fresh county-native certification from this visual enrichment.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Short usually erect dense terminal spike; at each rachis node a triad of ONE-flowered spikelets, the central fertile and lateral companions commonly sterile. Closely packed bristle-like glumes make the little barley head appear bottlebrush-like.
morphology_keys.spikelets: Central fertile floret with short lemma awn, surrounded at the node by two smaller sterile lateral spikelets. Glumes usually straight/upright ~8–17 mm (broad FNA range); the small fertile lemma ~5–8.5 mm, awn ~3.5–9.5 mm; exact dimensions require 1-mm macro.
morphology_keys.leaf_collar: Small membranous ligule (often ~0.2–0.8 mm), AURICLES absent, and hairiness possible on leaf blades; compare real collar/shoot rather than incorrectly teaching auricles as universal in the barley family.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Hordeum jubatum (foxtail barley; native broadly to much of North America, including Texas in Kew state-scale account; LOCAL Hays status unreviewed) is usually PERENNIAL, with long broadly outward-fanning awnlike glumes (up to 85 mm) and a fluffy/nodding spike. H. pusillum is ANNUAL, with short relatively erect spike, straighter glumes ~8–17 mm and shorter awns. BOTH species have ONE-FLOWERED spikelet TRIADS, central fertile/laterals mainly sterile; this is a GENUS trait. Elymus wildryes have more than one flower per spikelet and generally two/sometimes more spikelets per rachis node. Introduced H. murinum has broad fanlike glume groups and often auricles; planted H. vulgare has robust head/cultivar variability; rye Secale cereale differs in spikelet arrangement. Count a real node and inspect glumes, not merely head fuzz.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Compare one complete fully mature head and an intact rooted basal shoot; magnify outer glumes at one central rachis node.
field_matrix.this_species: LITTLE is annual, short erect tight spike (~2–9 cm), shorter mostly straight/upright outer glumes (~8–17 mm) and a short awned central fertile lemma.
field_matrix.look_alike: FOXTAIL is usually perennial and commonly nodding; long fine awnlike GLUMES diverge widely (often 35–85 mm central spikelet glumes), making a very fluffy brush.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Short erect head with compact relatively straight glumes + annual root = LITTLE candidate. Giant spreading feathery head + established perennial crown = FOXTAIL candidate. Both have THREE spikelets per node.

field_matrix.taxon: Canada / Virginia wildrye — Elymus canadensis / E. virginicus
field_matrix.where_to_look: At ONE central rachis node, count attached SPIKELETS, then examine individual spikelets for FLORET number.
field_matrix.this_species: Hordeum = THREE one-flowered spikelets grouped at each node: middle fertile, laterals often sterile/reduced.
field_matrix.look_alike: Elymus usually TWO multiflowered spikelets at each node (occasionally more), with more than one lemma/floret inside each spikelet.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Count spikelets then florets. Three small one-flowered spikelets at a node favor BARLEY; paired MULTI-flowered spikelets favor WILDRYE.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Check degree of fanlike glume groups, actual glume margins and clasping auricles at leaf collar.
field_matrix.this_species: Little barley glumes relatively narrow, straight, close to the rachis; collar auricles absent.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced wall barley commonly makes larger wide-fanning awn and glume groups, with distinct auricles and hairy glume edges in some treatments.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Do not label little barley only from short bottlebrush appearance; magnify triad glumes and true collar.

field_matrix.taxon: Cultivated barley or rye — Hordeum vulgare / Secale cereale
field_matrix.where_to_look: Find full rooted plant, flowering head, a rachis node and mature cereal-size spikelets.
field_matrix.this_species: Small wild annual with dense compact bristly spike and Hordeum triads.
field_matrix.look_alike: Cultivated barley is often taller, stouter and more robust with cereal-grain heads; rye generally has solitary multi-flowered spikelets arranged along the axis rather than Hordeum triads.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Large planted cereal escape or singular multi-flowered rye spikelets warrant checking cultivar/horticultural history and mature flowering anatomy.

not_reliable_alone: Bristly spike or three units per node: BOTH Hordeum species share the triad.
Seasonal green growth: several cool-season native and introduced grasses share it.
Foxtail is native broadly to Texas; do not label it universally exotic simply because it forms weeds elsewhere.
Awn/glume measurements from one distant photograph without ruler.
A single broken terminal seedhead: you lose annual/perennial rooting and floret number.
Simple hairy/auriculate grass collar without actual Hordeum rachis node.

visual_comparison.title: Little barley versus foxtail barley — both have spikelet TRIADS
visual_comparison.subtitle: The existing Matt Lavin CC BY little-barley photo has two previously pixel-checked gross arrows. A separately licensed Montana foxtail-barley photo shows the dramatic spreading mature glume awns for context; the two-species native-range status is NOT inferred from photos.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: LITTLE = small upright erect SPIKE + short straight GLUMES + ANNUAL. FOXTAIL = big nodding FEATHER + very long SPLAYED GLUMES + usually PERENNIAL. BOTH have 3 spikelets/node.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Little barley — learn the triad, then compare the foxtail
steps: FIRST: find the annotated SHORT narrow erect SPIKE and relatively close-lying AWNS on the existing little barley photo.

SECOND: in your local rooted plant, isolate ONE central rachis node—Hordeum has THREE grouped spikelets, a fertile middle and smaller lateral companions. This detail is NOT shown in the existing close enough for species-proof arrows.
THIRD: compare the foxtail photo below; mature Hordeum jubatum has MUCH longer glume awns spread broadly outward around a soft, often drooping head.
FOURTH: inspect the whole ROOTED base. H. pusillum is an annual; H. jubatum normally perennial. Photograph mature outer glumes with 1-mm ruler.
FIFTH: before calling it barley rather than wildrye, compare Elymus's MULTIFLORED paired spikelets. If structures cannot be resolved, use Hordeum sp. or Triticeae grass candidate.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: 3 spikelets per node is a Hordeum shared character. To separate the two, use mature GLUME length/direction + WHOLE spike posture + annual/perennial root crown together.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Only the installed little barley image has source-verified original arrows; neither has verified pixel-resolved node triads or leaf collar macros. Do not claim Hays occurrence of comparison-only foxtail barley.
